column4: A known-answer question recalls that the heavens and earth were once joined and God split them apart; the divine opening of something compact into newly habitable space is a large-scale analogue of the section's concrete action.

The youths are promised that their Lord will spread His mercy for them and prepare facility in their affair, joining divine spreading, beneficiary-marking, and a task made manageable just as the section does.
God removes the rancor within the inhabitants' breasts, showing relief as an actual extraction of harmful inward content from the bodily container the section opens.
God removes rancor from people's breasts and sets them face to face as brothers, a repeated direct picture of inward space cleared of what had occupied it.
Whether speech is kept secret or spoken aloud, God knows what breasts contain; the ayah tightly joins hidden speech, disclosure, and the breast as interior, the section's three linked concerns.
God knows what breasts conceal, directly corresponding to the hidden interior that the section's action of opening makes accessible.
Those who dispute God's signs harbor only an unattainable greatness in their breasts, supplying a specific harmful content that shows why the direction and filling of inward space matter.
The whisperer places suggestion into people's breasts, a malign form of something entering the inner space whose openness the section refuses to treat as good in itself.
At Hunayn the earth becomes narrow for the believers despite all its breadth, repeating the precise paradox that outward width can coexist with experienced constriction.
When the messengers reach Lot, he is distressed and feels straitened in his capacity to protect them; the bodily idiom of too little room parallels the section's chest made fit for a hard mission.
The arrival of the messengers again makes Lot distressed and straitened in capacity before they reassure him, a repeated mission scene of constriction answered by divine aid.
The record is set down and found to have omitted nothing small or great, making an opened document's formerly contained detail fully visible in the way the section describes unfolding and disclosure.
God will fold the sky like a scroll, the exact physical reversal of the section's underlying movement from something folded and compact to something spread open.
Each opponent wanting pages spread open for him is a concrete occurrence of an opened written object; its link is limited to the section's physical spreading action rather than its chest or mission.
The people found between the barriers can scarcely understand speech, a specific communicative closure against which the section's dictionary sense of opening difficult words becomes visible.
God teaches the human being clear expression, presenting intelligible speech as a divine enabling of the faculty whose knot Moses asks to have loosened.
The revelation comes in a clear Arabic tongue, giving the positive speech state corresponding to a tongue released so that its hearers can understand.
Moses explicitly says he fears that Pharaoh's people will deny him; this supplies the named fear immediately before his breast constricts and his tongue fails to proceed in 26:13.
God answers Moses' fear with a refusal of its conclusion and commands both brothers to go with the signs, completing the movement from constricted reluctance to divinely enabled mission.
Moses recalls having killed one of Pharaoh's people and fears being killed, identifying the danger immediately before he asks for the more eloquent Aaron to support his speech.
Moses says the requested chest-room, ease, and help will let them glorify God much, giving a Godward purpose to the capacity requested in the preceding prayer.
Remembering God much is the second stated purpose of Moses' requested enabling, anticipating the section's movement from expanded capacity toward the Lord.
After the command to answer chest-constriction with praise and prostration, continued worship carries that redirection toward the Lord through the remainder of life.
God explicitly intends ease for people and does not intend hardship, stating as a divine purpose the same ease-versus-difficulty relation that follows the section's opened breast.
After prescribing purification, God says He does not wish to place constriction upon believers but to purify them and complete His favor, tying absence of حَرَج to an enabling benefaction.
After the account of ʿAd, the refrain again says God made the Quran easy for remembrance, confirming that the accessible-speech claim is deliberately repeated rather than incidental.
After Thamud's destruction, the same declaration that the Quran was made easy for remembrance repeats the section's connection between divine speech and facilitated reception.
After Lot's people, the repeated making-easy of the Quran supplies another distinct contextual occurrence of speech rendered accessible for remembrance.
Whatever mercy God opens for people cannot be withheld, making divine opening an act that creates access to a beneficial content rather than an empty expansion.

God opens for heedless people the gates of everything until they exult, then seizes them suddenly; the harmful opening sharply supports the section's claim that openness alone does not determine its value.

If God expanded provision without measure, people would transgress, so He sends it down in due measure; this is a specific nonlexical case where expansion itself can harm unless its content and measure are right.
During the siege, eyes swerve and hearts reach throats, making fear a bodily obstruction of breath and speech comparable to the section's chest as the felt site of constriction.
On the approaching day, hearts are at throats while people choke back their anguish, another explicit bodily scene of inward pressure opposite to a breast given room.

The verse uses the رغبة verb concerning marrying orphan women without an expressed directional preposition; because the construction has been read as desire for or aversion from marriage, it cautiously illustrates why the root's direction must be specified.
In the same opening-victory passage, God sends tranquility into believers' hearts so that faith increases, concretely naming a beneficial content placed within after divine opening.

The known-answer question “Did We not make the earth a resting place?” recalls a completed divine act that creates usable room for its beneficiaries, echoing both the section's rhetoric and spatial action.
God promises to make the Prophet recite so that he does not forget, another direct divine enabling of prophetic speech alongside the section's opened chest and loosened tongue.

The question about telling believers what God had opened to the speakers can carry the sense of disclosing revealed knowledge; if that reading is intended, it tentatively parallels the section's speech sense of making hidden meaning visible.

The Helpers find no inward need in their breasts concerning what others receive and prefer the emigrants over themselves, showing spacious moral capacity through the absence of a constricting content.
